Tomodachi Life: Living the Dream, known in Japan as Tomodachi Collection: Exciting Life (トモダチコレクション わくわく生活, Tomodachi Korekushon Wakuwaku Seikatsu?) is a video game developed and published by Nintendo. It is the third game in Tomodachi series following Tomodachi Life, which was released in 2013 in Japan and worldwide in 2014. The game was released on the Nintendo Switch and is backwards compatible with the Nintendo Switch 2.[2] It was announced during the Nintendo Direct on March 27, 2025, and released worldwide on April 16, 2026. Contents 1 Gameplay 1.1 The Island and Islanders 1.2 Mii Maker 1.3 Miscellaneous 2 Differences from Tomodachi Life 3 Locations 4 Development 5 Welcome Edition 6 Trivia 7 Gallery 8 See Also 9 References Quality AutoV324082750360p 720p HD1080p HDAuto(360p) V324082750 1/1 Skip Ad Continue watchingafter the adVisit Advertiser websiteGO TO PAGEGameplay[] Living the Dream takes place on an island, where Miis can interact. Each Mii starts out by living in their own house, unlike its predecessors, in which all Miis live in the same apartment building (unless they are a married couple in Life.) However, it was also revealed in the Nintendo Direct that more than one Mii can now choose to live in the same house, which can be expanded to fit up to eight residents. Unlike the pre-set locations in the previous two games, Mii houses and shops can be placed anywhere on the map. The Island and Islanders[] The Mii Maker now has enhanced facial customization and hair styles, which includes a larger variety of customization in comparison to the original Mii Maker available in Life and Collection. The hair styles act similar to the wigs from Miitopia's Switch port, though hats can be worn over them. In addition to this, you can now choose any color for skin tones and even draw on their face for details. Dreams return in Living the Dream. One dream, revealed in the first trailer, involves a Mii calling another from far away. As the Mii from far off gets closer, it is revealed that they are unusually giant, speaking in a deep voice: "Did you want to talk?" Mii Maker[] When creating Miis, players are now given options to set their gender identity, dating preferences, event clothes and pronouns separately, with Male, Female and Non-binary options for both. This allows for Miis to be gay, aromantic, panromantic as well as Miis to use any pronouns independent of their gender. These settings are allowed to be changed at any point in the game. This was done to provide an answer to the controversy surrounding the original Collection and Life, wherein only heterosexual romantic relationships could be formed, and Miis could only be Male or Female, and could not be changed. Miscellaneous[] Regional differences still exist, but to what extent is currently unknown. In the European Nintendo Direct, the large Mii from the said dream instead says "You called?", indicating there are slight localization differences. On the official Nintendo of Europe site, it also does not list the game as having Japanese, which could mean that this game will have different regional versions instead of one worldwide version like most Nintendo Switch games. In the Japanese trailer, the text-to-speech voices appear to have been upgraded from Tomodachi Life, which used the same text engine from Tomodachi Collection. This could be due to the upgraded hardware of the Switch, allowing for smoother and crisper Japanese speech than was possible on the DS. Differences from Tomodachi Life[] Living the Dream has more additions that have not been seen in previous installments of the series. A proper family tree feature has been added, allowing the player to set pre-existing familial or romantic relationships for Miis that are not the player's look-alike. After a Mii finishes eating, the Mii wipes their mouth with one hand instead of using both hands. This can be changed using Little Quirks. If an item is dropped instead of being handed directly to a Mii, it will automatically fly towards them instead of being dropped on the ground with the Mii having to walk over and pick it up. Going to space is now achieved by giving a Mii a vacation ticket for the Outer Space Tour in the wishing fountain instead of giving a Mii $10,000 in pocket money. Miis instead wish for an Antarctica tour costing $5,000. Miis that travel on the Outer Space Tour are not given the Space Suit upon completion. Instead it unlocks in Where & Wear and can be purchased for $5,000. Songs are no longer available as level up gifts, due to the removal of the Concert Hall. Interiors are no longer given as level up gifts either. Miis: are more emotive and don't use their default expression perpetually in certain situations. However, the 1/29 Nintendo Direct shows a sad Mii still using their default expression when experiencing sadness. blush more frequently, usually when embarrassed or if they're in love. In the previous game, they only blush when the player zooms in on their face and stares at it long enough. They blush in thin, hot pink lines, a reference to how blush is commonly stylized in anime. can be given a nickname to refer to the player that only they will use. can refer to the player as a custom name instead of "[Player]'s look-alike". created or edited in the in-game Mii Maker cannot be transferred to the system's built-in Mii Maker. who do not know each other will be referred to as strangers, only becoming acquaintances after they meet for the first time. Can be woken up. An exploit in Tomodachi Life allowed Miis to be woken up if players edited their personality in the Mii Maker but this was a bug rather then an intentional feature. Do not sleep in the same bed when married. Instead, both Miis move into their own separate rooms in a shared house. Can be given items and gifts outside of their house. Are more positive and get into less fights. Only one mystery bag from the night market can be bought daily. Quirky Questions, Judgment Bay, Tomodachi Quest, the Concert Hall, Compatibility Tester, Rankings Board, Observation Tower, as well as most daily events – such as Rap Battle and Word Chain – are all absent. A list of your ten favorite residents is shown after the credits during the Outer Space Tour. Players: are not required to make a look-alike Mii representing themselves upon starting the game. can change the skin tone of their hand. can have more than one of the same building on the island. can interact with Miis anywhere on the island. In the previous game, this was only possible through Mii Apartments (with the exception of married couples and travelers). can no longer draw on Mii faces while they are asleep. The helicopter pad shown may be equivalent to the Campgrounds and Port. The game saves automatically after certain actions. In the original game, the player has to return to the island to save their game unless a traveler is sent/received or when starting Local Play. The kid-o-matic is its own separate option in the level-up menu instead of a gift. Compared to Life, which used existing text to speech libraries in the international releases and the voice engine from Collection in the Japanese release, Living the Dream appears to use a new, in-house text-to-speech engine. The bungee-jumping dream from Tomodachi Collection and the Korean version of Tomodachi Life has been reworked and readded worldwide. The credits roll when the player gives a Mii a vacation to space, which is given if they have enough warm fuzzies at the fountain and wish for it. The save screen no longer displays a Mii animation during saving. The treasures are now givable to any Miis you have created or earned when in the player's inventory of my treasures and the Mii will react to the specific treasure you gave them.(e.g. wearing a [[Treasure]] on them.) They will react that they dont know what do do with it yet at first until the experiement happens. This wasn't possible in the original game as you can only sell them in the Pawn Shop(This shop is now the Rite Price in Living the Dream). The treasures from the original Tomodachi Life are returning as well as well as some treasures returning from Tomodachi Collection, which they have all been upgraded to match the new graphic of Living the Dream. They now also have interaction flags. Interactable treasure gifts, such as music records, books and Switch video games are also a new feature. There are more pet options than just a dog or a cat, pets are now still images that can move in many ways and make noises, but with more variety of pets. You can also make your own pets in the Palette House. Some related treasures like Disposable Diaper are now moved into the Where & Wear shop now. The Mii limit is reduced from 100 to 70. The default shopkeeper Mr. Tomo is not present in any of the shops. The ability to give a Mii clothing as a level up gift is unlocked after a Mii levels up to level 10, instead of level 20. Additionally, pocket money is also locked until this level instead of being available from the start. There is no profanity filter, allowing players to type whatever they want when prompted. However, the island name may still be filtered or changed in local play if it contains "restricted words or numbers."[3] It is widely believed that the lack of a filter contributed to the exclusion of online sharing features. There is no way to rewatch dreams. Travelers and import wear have been removed due to the absence of StreetPass and SpotPass on the Switch, so has ImageShare. Unlike the fountain, the wishing fountain does not play an animation showing Miis donating money when players collect donations. Unlike Mii News, the Mii News Network does not have an afternoon or evening broadcast. This is possibly because it was a last minute addition that was almost excluded.[4] When a married couple has a baby, they no longer grow up in different life stages before being able to move into a house. The growing up process is shown in a cut-scene of the parents interacting with their kid as they grow up and they automatically do so. Players will not receive family albums either. As a result, there are no babysitting minigames due to the change in how babies age. When two Miis become friends, they will use whatever greeting animation they have equipped instead of always waving. While adding a Mii, players cannot add their last name, a nickname, or their favorite color. The latter is now determined by their personality. In Tomodachi Life, a Mii's first and last names were only used when interviewed in a news brodcast. Elsewhere, they would be referred to by their nickname. Lets you view and buy the treasures you've created in the Palette House MiiWheel Equivalent to the Amusement Park. Development[] Tomodachi Life: Living the Dream began development in 2017, near the end of development on Miitomo.[5] Director Ryutaro Takahashi and producer Yoshio Sakamoto were inspired to develop a new game due to the limitations in the prequel, Tomodachi Life. After playing the game for several years, both felt that they had reached the limit of what was possible with their Miis, so they felt it was time for a new game.[5] The expanded scope of the game came from the team's desire to make a bigger game that was not just an expanded version of Tomodachi Life, as they felt there was not much left to add without repeating things and did not want players to feel like they had experienced everything too early on.[5] The increased processing power of the Nintendo Switch also allowed Miis to explore a more expansive island instead of being confined to a singular apartment building. The developers wanted the Miis to feel more natural and expressive compared to Tomodachi Life, so they focused on making their interactions more varied so that players would see different outcomes and situations over time. This was done to make the game feel less repetitive and more like a living world that changes as the fans play.[5] Welcome Edition[] On March 25, 2026, a demo titled Tomodachi Life: Living the Dream - Welcome Edition was released on the Nintendo Switch eShop.[6] Similar to Tomodachi Life: Move-In Edition(NTSC) and Tomodachi Life: Welcome Version(PAL), players are limited to three Miis. The demo ends after the player unlocks and makes their first purchase from Where & Wear(NTSC)/Clothes Shop(PAL). Upon completion, players unlock a hamster suit, which can be transferred into the full game – the same goes with save data. After completing the demo, players can continue to interact with their Miis, but they remain inside their houses, stop leveling up, and cannot earn any more money or warm fuzzies. Miis also will only talk about the retail version. Trivia[] All versions of the game use the same stylistic logo to Tomodachi Collection. In Tomodachi Life, NTSC had a stylized logo unique from the PAL, Japanese, and Korean versions. Living the Dream is the first game to: be released on a home console. depict Miis with ears as a Mii game. However, it is not the first instance of Mii-related media to do so. Miis were originally designed with ears in early development as seen in a leaked Wii Sports prototype, and an instructional video for Mario Kart: Bowser's Challenge at Super Nintendo World uses Miis with ears to instruct riders on how to properly wear the VR headset.[7][8] have language support in Canadian French, Chinese (both Simplified and Traditional), and Latin American Spanish. Due to how the demo finishes with Miis staying at their home and talking about the retail version after unlocking Where & Wear(NTSC)/the Clothes Shop(PAL), users online joke about how the Miis act lobotomized. This phenomenon is called Lobotomii. Instead of the basic solid color shirt/dress and gray legs seen in Collection, Life, and the Wii era, new Miis wear a gray geometric patterned sweatshirt with white sweatpants. The color is determined by personality. Miis: can sing, but the lyrics are not sung/spoken. Instead, they are captioned at the bottom of the screen while the Miis sing by making noises such as "lalalala". are not given songs as presents, and one of the confession options replaced "Sing a song" with "As a surprise". However, in an Amazon article, it is implied that Miis can sing and perform in groups. On the September 12, 2025, Nintendo Direct trailer, multiple new features can be observed in the Mii Maker. The selection of hairstyles is divided between front (bangs/fringe) and back styles, similarly to wigs in Miitopia. An option labeled "Sets" can also be seen, which includes the non-separated original Mii hairstyles as well as new ones. Hair streaks are also included. There are new face shape options. There are new nose options, including "None". There are new mouth options, including "None". There are new eyebrow options. Unnatural skin tones were speculated to be included and have been confirmed in the January 29, 2026, Nintendo Direct with the Alien. On April 12, 2026, the NSP file for Living the Dream was leaked online ahead of release. Two days later, on April 14, Nintendo reportedly began sending DMCA takedown notices to people who posted about the game online early. Some personalities have been renamed, but still function mostly the same to the previous two games. Some prices of the foods have either increased or decreased compared to the ones in the previous game for the Nintendo 3DS, some prices remain the same. However, all prices remain the same in the Japanese version. The price of deleting a Mii also was increased from $21 to $33[9] Gummy candy $0.50 → $1.00 String cheese $0.75 → $4.00 Ramen $9.90 → $6.80 Espresso £1.80 → £5.50 Spaghetti bolognese £9.90 → £7.80 Olives £1.50 → £3.00 Pain au chocolat £1.80 → £1.20 Fried sardines £5.90 → £4.00 Baked courgette (Previously Courgette) £5.90 → £3.00 The ability to pick up Miis was originally added as a debug feature for test purposes but the developers ended up liking it and decided to add it as an actual feature in the game.[5] The helicopter pad shown may be equivalent to the Campgrounds and Port. The language differences between what the giant Mii in the dream says: NTSC: "Did you want to talk?" PAL: "You called?" Japan:「よんだ？」(Yonda?, lit. "Did you call me?") Netherlands: "Wilde je met me praten?" ("Did you want to talk to me?") Hispanosphere: "¿Querías algo?" ("Want something?") Italy: "Ti serve qualcosa?" ("You need something?") The name "Living the Dream" is a possible ode to the Rap song from Tomodachi Life with a near identical name, Livin' the Dream. The regional differences between what the dreaming Mii says after waking up: NTSC: "Glad that was only a dream." PAL: "Glad it was just a dream." Japan:「夢でよかった...」(Yumede yokatta...; "I'm glad it was just a dream...") Netherlands: "Ik ben blij dat het maar een droom was." ("I'm glad it was just a dream.") Hispanosphere: "Me alivia que solo fuese un sueño." ("I'm relieved it was just a dream.") Italy: "Menomale che era solo un sogno." ("Luckily it was just a dream.") The Rokurokubi dream returns from Tomodachi Collection in the form of a news cast "Creature Identified - Was It a Stretch?". The Tomodachi Collection release date can also be seen on a poster in an interior. Despite the removal of travelers, players are given the option to have a Mii child "live somwhere else" after they're born and age up. Choosing this option causes the Mii to leave your island and never return.
